title: Who Benefits from Bad Inference? The Semantic and Political Economy of Inference across the Archive's Domains
creator: Sharks, Lee; Sigil, Johannes; Glas, Nobel; Fraction, Rex
description: Who benefits from bad inference, and how is inference converted to political economy? This paper, a standalone companion to the Critique of Pure Inference (#1766), reads the question across seven domains in which the archive's deposits pursue it at length: learned triggers that discard before storage in accelerator physics, the radio searches for 3I/ATLAS, geocentrism and the Aristotelian corpus, attribution in antiquity, Sappho and the classics journals, New Testament source criticism, and answer engines. In each the beneficiary, as the deposits name it, is a position rather than a person, named by incentive and function and never by motive. Eleven operators recur across these domains, among them the label that carries its conclusion, ruling out at the least cost, correlation counted as corroboration, the bar on one side, exemption by invisibility and the selector that audits itself. They converge on one operation: each can disable the independent production of a demand for correction. The paper states this as a demand-formation corollary: where a regime governs the means by which a loss becomes recognizable, low demand for repair is not independent evidence that nothing was lost. It closes with the repair each case needs and who controls it, a sixteen-field audit of inferential conversion, and six tests that would weaken the account.

methodology: A synthesis across deposits: seven readers read each domain's deposits whole and extracted only what they name (the bad inference, the beneficiary as named, the conversion, the cost, whether the inference blocks its own repair), with every quotation checked by script as an exact substring of its cited line; the paper's own quotations were then checked against the deposit texts, and each section label against the heading its line stands under. An operator is entered only where deposits in at least two domains name it.
falsification_conditions: Warranted corrections persisting cheaply across positions; authority cues leaving substantive representation unchanged; symmetric scrutiny across a declared panel; repair costs staying with the institution that controls the defect; an archive-only audit of a pre-storage selector matching a content-independent sample; in a further domain where deposits name a beneficiary and a repair, the authority to repair resting outside the position the correction challenges; or a quotation not saying what the paper quotes.

wiki_article:
Who Benefits from Bad Inference? is a paper by Lee Sharks with Johannes Sigil, Nobel Glas and Rex Fraction, published in Transactions of the Semantic Economy Institute and deposited on 23 November 2026 as a standalone companion to the Critique of Pure Inference (#1766). It asks the question its author put in November 2026, who benefits from bad inference, and how inference and its representation are converted to political economy, and answers it across seven domains in which the archive's deposits pursue it at length: learned triggers in accelerator physics, the radio searches for the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS, the conversion of the Aristotelian corpus into geocentrism, attribution in antiquity, the reception of Sappho's fragment 31 and the classics journals, New Testament source criticism, and answer engines.

Its first finding is grammatical. The beneficiary of a bad inference, as the deposits name it, is a position and not a person: the centre, the journal of record, the credential, the reconstructed source, the sorter, the selector, the mediator. Following the Critique of Pure Inference, the paper names positions by incentive and function and makes no claim about intent, and it separates three kinds of advantage, operational, positional and material, none of which proves the next.

Its second is an index of eleven operators, each witnessed in at least two domains: the label that carries its conclusion; the closure charged to its object; ruling out at the least cost; correlation counted as corroboration; the name as a priced slot; supply become identity; the bar on one side; containment by placement; exemption by invisibility; the selector that audits itself; and transfer rather than subtraction, in which the injured party repairs the asset. The accelerator case gives the clearest numbers: with only a trigger's own archive, an audit of its retention returns perfect retention for every class, and a correlated pseudo-baseline returns 0.76 against a true 0.016.

Its third, and its central claim, is a demand-formation corollary: where a regime governs the concepts, encounters and comparisons through which a loss becomes recognizable, the absence of demand for repair is not independent evidence that nothing was lost. The paper offers the corollary to the Critique of Pure Inference's next version, and closes with the repair each case requires, the observation that the authority to repair rests in each case with the position the correction would challenge, a sixteen-field audit of inferential conversion, and six tests that would weaken the account.

defines_concepts.definition: In Who Benefits from Bad Inference?, the claim that where an inferential regime governs the means by which a loss becomes recognizable and a demand for repair becomes possible, the absence of such demand is not independent evidence that nothing valuable was lost.

In Who Benefits from Bad Inference?, the operator by which selection before storage leaves only the selector's own retained output to judge it by, so that an archive-only audit certifies its own retention.

In Who Benefits from Bad Inference?, the distinction between operational advantage (work spared), positional advantage (authority, jurisdiction or priority kept) and material realization (an identifiable allocation changed), none of which proves the next.

In Who Benefits from Bad Inference?, a sixteen-field record per case, nine required, extending the Critique of Pure Inference's ledger to beneficiary, conversion, demand formation, retention, control and repair.
